related: issue #102718

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

After the reflector obtains the ObjectList through ListAndWatch, it will obtain the Object list through ExtractList (internally obtain the list of objects through go-reflect) and store it in Indexer. Assuming that an Object in the List does not change (). Then the memory occupied by the entire ObjectList cannot be released. Although most of the data in this List is out of date.

We remove the dependency on ObjectList through Alloc && Set (**ShallowCopy**) on the object. Help golang runtime gc this section does not need to use memory.

pr_comments: I'm not convinced we should deep copy at all. But definitely it shouldn't go here, there are other callers of this code path than just the watch cache.

> I'm not convinced we should deep copy at all. But definitely it shouldn't go here, there are other callers of this code path than just the watch cache.

@lavalamp 

Thank you for your suggestion ~ 😄

I find a more suitable place to add the relevant logic.

/cc @liggitt @wojtek-t @lavalamp
/triage accepted

/ping @lavalamp 

Hi @lavalamp . In order not to destroy the original ExtractList. I added ExtractWithAlloc. And instead of using DeepCopy, a shallow copy of the newly generated object is done by using reflect.New and reflect.Value.Set. The map and slice in the newly generated object will share the same memory space with the elements in the list. Only the basic types of golang fields such as int and string will allocate memory. After my tests, it can work well (unit tests are being written), and I hope to get some suggestions from you on the solution. grateful.

This still double-allocates for some amount of time, it's too late.

I'm actually not even convinced that deep copy is enough, are e.g. strings copied or are they still references to the original deserialized data?

A correct fix is going to be very invasive, which is why I'm questioning that the benefit would be high enough.

Some clarifications are necessary here:

Take `corev1.ConfigMapList` as an example (for the sake of convenience, I directly copied the relevant part of the code to prevent jumping around):

```golang
type ConfigMapList struct {
         ....
	Items []ConfigMap
}

type ConfigMap struct {
	metav1.TypeMeta `json:",inline"`
	metav1.ObjectMeta `json:"metadata,omitempty" protobuf:"bytes,1,opt,name=metadata"`
        ....
	Data map[string]string `json:"data,omitempty" protobuf:"bytes,2,rep,name=data"`
}

func (in *ConfigMap) DeepCopyObject() runtime.Object {
       ...
}
```

Items elements are all ConfigMap, ConfigMap does not implement runtime.Object, (the receiver of the DeepCopyObject method is *ConfigMap), so we need to use *ConfigMap.

The return value of our `ExtractList` is `[]runtime.Object`, so we have the following available:

1. Get the pointer of the ConfigMap.Items[i] element directly (the current implementation), but this will cause the Slice of ConfigMapList.Items to not be released

2. DeepCopy (Deprecated): Causes double memory consumption, ps: Not only will golang-basic type [int, string,] field values ​​(Kind, APIVersion, Name, UID, ...) be copied, when encountering To Data, or Labels, Annotations field type is Map[string]string will also be copied. 

3. Alloc a new ConfigMap, and assign a value to it. Execute code similar to the following:

`ret := configMapList.Items[0]`

Only the fields of the basic type (int, string... mentioned above) will be copied here, and the Data field will point to configMapList.Items[0].Data. When go-runtime executes the gc-routine, if configMapList.Items[0] has no related references. will be released. But since Data is referenced by ret.Data at the same time. This memory will not be freed.

> Here is a very strange question, why do method 1 and method 3 have the same number of allocations in the benchmark results?

This is because the following code exists in ExtractList:

````golang
func ExtractList(obj runtime.Object) ([]runtime.Object, error) {
	....
	for i := range list {
		raw := items.Index(i)
                
		switch item := raw.Interface().(type) {
		....
       ....
````

`items := raw.Interface().(type)` The code here has actually done an Alloc Object && Set to the ConfigMap

However, ExtractListWithAlloc determines the type by comparing raw.Type. When it is determined that the current Object is a ConfigMap, Alloc creates a new Configmap and assigns it a value. So it can not only guarantee the number of memory allocations, but also avoid directly referencing the Items list.

> The map and slice in the newly generated object will share the same memory space with the elements in the list. Only the basic types of golang fields such as int and string will allocate memory.

non-pointer struct fields (like ObjectMeta, Spec, and Status) will also be allocated. I don't think ConfigMap is a good example to benchmark… deeply nested high-cardinality objects with struct fields like Pod and Node are a better test for the cost of a shallow copy

I think we can actually fix the execution time hit by doing the type check during the list assign:

```
// shallow copy to avoid retaining a reference to the original list item
new := reflect.New(raw.Type())
new.Elem().Set(raw)
// assign to list and type-assert
list[i], ok = new.Interface().(runtime.Object)
if !ok {
	// unexpected failure on type assertion
	return nil, fmt.Errorf("%v: item[%v]: Expected object, got %#v(%s)", obj, i, raw.Interface(), raw.Kind())
}
```

Update: About EachListItem

The elements in EachListItem are not of type Pointer and Interface to take the address, 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.25/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/meta/help.go#L133-L146

so `switch item := raw.Interface().(type)` will only allocate a pointer with a very small space. So our EachListItems are consistent with the master. Just added this variant of alloc.

ps: Golang's type-assert is *more efficient* than reflect.

issue_context.title: Reflector retains initial list result for a long time
issue_context.body:
### What happened?

The result of initial list in Reflector is kept in the memory until the last element in the items list hasn't been changed. 

In practice this can be a long time, e.g. there can be some stable pod that are running for days, in configmaps there is a kube-root-ca.crt which stays there forever.

This problem is described here: https://go.dev/blog/slices-intro#a-possible-gotcha

IIUC this affects both:
* clients using informers/Reflectors
* kube-apiserver which is using the same Reflector to initialize watch cache

This means e.g. when all (but 1) elements are frequently updated, the memory usage is 2x the state size (the initial size + current size).

### What did you expect to happen?

When the objects are deleted from the cluster, the memory consumption of the Reflector drops.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

* Create cluster with 1GB state of significant size (e.g. by creating 1000 configmaps of size 1M each)
* Start informer (e.g. I was using https://gist.github.com/mborsz/8964c84b298ee63c7153190d608a7464)
* Observe memory usage (it should be around ~1GB as expected)
  * Sample [pprof](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2559168/197553760-cfd8a8f0-0996-4ee7-8f8c-5ea72e06bf8d.png)
* Remove 99% of the state
* [issue] Observe memory usage (it stays around ~1GB, despite state taking ~10M)
  * Sample [pprof](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2559168/197555163-adff7e50-e0db-4c75-8397-929b08dc9c08.png)
* Recreate the state (with the same name)
* [issue] The memory usage grows to ~2G
  * Sample [pprof](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2559168/197557325-f3aef1f3-c003-4f17-83db-5aac06ab5643.png)


### Anything else we need to know?

This seems to be consequence of the:
* ConfigMapList using []ConfigMap type (not []*ConfigMap)
* Reflector taking pointer to those objects https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/fe9d04763b94366a7a80a1ef3d9f83337eac722e/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/meta/help.go#L195-L200
* If any of the elements is in use, the entire Items is kept in the memory.

The naive fix would be to create a DeepCopy before storing data in Reflector, but this requires careful implementation to avoid increasing memory usage at the beginning (as we can easily have a list in Items and a deep copied list at the same time).

comments: Note that `[]runtime.Object` is essentially already a list of pointers, this can be addressed earlier just by making sure that the pointers don't all point into the same chunk of memory. No?

@lavalamp, yes.

The problem is that it's allocated as a single chunk in ConfigMapList implementation and to split them to separate memory obejcts we need to either deepcopy them (proposed in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/102565/files) or change the ConfigMapList to use pointer type for Items elements (I would assume it's infeasible, right?).

I wouldn't say it's 100% infeasible. The problem with any fix to this issue is that this is a rare-ish condition and fixing it will make the ordinary condition worse, either at runtime or in the codebase.

> this is a rare-ish condition

IIUC this shouldn't be that rare: correct me if I'm wrong, but  for me it looks like any client (including kube-apiserver itself) using reflector, watching resource type of high cardinality will keep the initial state forever (assuming that there is some object that isn't changing [*])

[*] It's not clear how often is the not changing object condition, but it shouldn't be very hard for resources like pods or configmaps, secrets which tends to be large in size.

> the ordinary condition worse, (...) in the codebase.

Are you referring to the pointer Items solution? Can you help me understanding why it's worse then the current state? Is it a cost of migration (which I assume can be huge) or something else?

> any client (including kube-apiserver itself) using reflector, watching resource type of high cardinality will keep the initial state forever

But making a deep copy of everything doubles up initial memory usage all the time for everyone.

We should do some research on this issue:

After reflector obtains ObjectList through ListAndWatch, it obtains the Object list through ExtractList (internally obtains the object list through go-reflect) and stores it in Indexer. Suppose an Object in the List has not changed (). Then the memory occupied by the entire ObjectList cannot be released. Although most of the data on this list is **out of date**. This can lead to more memory consumption than expected on some common objects with large numbers (eg: pods, nodes, configmaps...).

We submitted a PR #113362 to try and fix this.

Remove the dependency on ObjectList by DeepCopying the object. Help golang runtime gc not need to use memory.

> > any client (including kube-apiserver itself) using reflector, watching resource type of high cardinality will keep the initial state forever
> 
> But making a deep copy of everything doubles up initial memory usage all the time for everyone.


emmm... Is such that. This modification will cause a memory spike (as you said, double the amount of memory required for initialization), but I think the cost is worth it. As the running time increases, only real-time objects remain in memory, which has obvious advantages when the number of objects is large.
I'm reasonably sure many large clusters wouldn't be able to survive double the memory spike on startup.

Hi everyone, I submitted a PR #113362  to try and fix the issue. The core is to make a shallow copy through (reflect.New and reflect.Value.Set) instead of DeepCopy (to avoid the double memory usage problem mentioned by @lavalamp)

Several modifications are included:

- Faster `ExtractList`, implemented by comparing reflect.Type directly, not through `switch item := raw.Interface().(type)` (avoid a shallow copy)
- Added `ExtractListWithAlloc` by a shallow copy to remove dependencies between objects and the Items slice to help gc
